be relevant to the incident, now they have log, metric, deployment, and code change history

Observability's tools detects and alerts on usage patterns outside of normal activity. It has had

and don't require as many people to resolve. The operations and application teams are much

before has been mitigated and even started to decline.

Perhaps the best result of all the work is an improved reputation for ACME Financial Services.

Summary
In this chapter, we have followed our fictional company, ACME Financial Services, as they
found themselves in a difficult and unmanageable situation after completing their cloud
migration. Operational costs had jumped and their old observability practices were no longer
working. They had to find a way to address their problems before they resulted in serious
damage to the company. This required forming a group to investigate and learn about new
observability practices and tooling, evaluate new tools, plan company-wide improvements,
deploy new infrastructure, negotiate priorities, and get senior leadership support for the entire
plan. It was a herculean effort that affected the entire company and took many years to
complete, but the end result was a more efficient incident response process and, best of all,
improved company reputation.
This ended up only being the start of their journey. As with many complex problems, solving
one set of problems reveals additional problems that were hidden or not understood at the
start. One of the biggest drivers of the changes was cost control, and the observability working
group discovered that it is not as easy to reduce costs as they thought.
Cost was just one dimension of a much larger challenge. In this chapter, we discussed the
importance of making observability make sense by going from overwhelming data to
actionable information. In the next chapter, we'll look more at how an Internal Developer
Platform (IDP) helps organizations turn observability data into actionable information—a
lesson ACME Financial Services will also learn in future chapters.

A self-service platform is an IDP that enables the development teams using it to utilize features

Often just called the platform, an IDP provides centralized golden-path self-service to

An IDP approach to software delivery is typically a business decision taken to accelerate

being developed. When software application developers need to move fast, a self-service
platform can provide them with the competencies to quickly start shipping a product, but also

The purpose of an IDP is to unify the method by which highly repetitive tasks are accomplished
across the organization. Technology can replace people, taking dedicated release and
operations teams from individual development teams with duplicated repetitive tasks into a
central platform. This allows the development teams to spend their time focused on writing
software and not on the idx_5b35199f delivery mechanisms.

Kubernetes standardization
The Kubernetes API allows for object enrichment through the usage of labels and
annotations. Labels allow for objects to be idx_0b1934d1 selected by the value of the labels, effectively
making them a way of identifying related Kubernetes objects. Labels idx_a0d38e16 can be made available to
all cluster users via the app.kubernetes.io prefix and kept private to users if used without the
prefix. On the other hand, annotations are for storing non-identifying metadata and are
available to any user that has access to read the annotated object. In this context, identifying
means that the data can be used for searching and grouping objects. What would typically be
considered identifying data can be used in annotations, for example, to identify the pager
escalation for a workload, but it would need to be parsed by additional automation tools as
that is not the functionality of the Kubernetes API.
An example of a label is app.kubernetes.io/environment: staging, which could be used for
filtering or searching for all Kubernetes objects with the same labels. An annotation might have
information about the owning team or their Slack channel. The annotation can be used by
additional automation to direct idx_8fc21c19 data or alerts for the workload, and the staging label lets the
team know what environment the data belongs to. However, there are many other examples of
best practices. The following tables should be considered a source of ideas, not a

Kustomize
Kustomize is a configuration management tool included in Kubernetes by default that allows
users to generate idx_9fe9a9da configuration automatically.
For example, with Kustomize, you can idx_bcf19c19 use the annotation transformer to automatically apply
annotations to Kubernetes resources. This prevents mistakes or blocking of resource
deployment by ensuring the method for applying configuration lives on the cluster alongside
the workloads it is modifying. In the YAML for the Kustomize file, the methods for identifying
which workloads to select and modify are defined.
Kustomize's strength is its ability to crawl a directory and, with surgical precision, modify the
contents within.
Boilerplate code and templates
Boilerplate code is idx_379e9026 often supplied in a software development kit (SDK), typically as a
common library or function that developers can use to complete idx_a9f33dfb tasks. The Operator SDK for
building Kubernetes operators generates quite a bit of boilerplate to help fill in the basic
functions of an operator, and also includes the capability to generate observability
configurations by using boilerplate code to expose metrics that are considered a best practice;
see https://book.kubebuilder.io/reference/metrics-reference.html for more
information on those metrics.
Another example of boilerplate code comes idx_8180f2bf from the OpenTelemetry (OTel) SDK. This SDK

In Chapter 1, we discussed OTel and Prometheus for metrics collection, so we won't dive deep

Prometheus's templating capability leverages the Go templates package of Golang. There's
more than one place where templating is idx_e29d45ab usable, but the most common use is likely in the
alerting rules. This allows you to write alert rules once, for every Kubernetes resource kind on

annotations:
summary: "Pod {{ $labels.pod }} is crashing"

Pod {{ $labels.pod }} in namespace {{ $labels.namespace }}
is restarting frequently on node {{ $labels.node }}.
Prometheus templates can also be used to add the label and annotation metadata to metrics
and alerts, ensuring proper idx_eddde345 data enrichment during query and export. Typically, this idx_82d913b4 would be

Helm templates
Helm is called the Kubernetes idx_dea3b639 package manager and provides robust tooling for managing

Prometheus, also uses Golang templates, with additional functionality written into the engine.
Helm manages inheritance idx_15018472 within the templating, allowing charts to have customizations but
also to inherit characteristics from parent charts, allowing developers to leverage the power of
templates while maintaining flexibility where needed.

monitoring stack would be inserted into the Terraform .tf files directly. The " as code " portion
of " infrastructure as code " means that the deployment of the infrastructure is repeatable, and

chunks.content:
there's a single source of truth for how to do it. Terraform code is organized into modules,
allowing idx_69bfcd22 for small and independent changes within the code base, somewhat similar to Helm
charts. Modules support variables so that they're reusable across multiple teams within a
single organization. Modules are not templates, because Terraform tracks what piece of
infrastructure is owned by which module. In other words, it maintains a state for what it
manages and compares the actual state to the desired state before it takes any actions. On the
surface, this may not seem different from Helm, but Helm relies on the state management
provided by Kubernetes and does not maintain its own record of state, which is a key capability
of Terraform. Like many of the tools we've described, there's a large community around
Terraform, and there are many community-built Terraform modules available at https://
registry.terraform.io to help you idx_9c7c18ce get started.
OpenTofu
OpenTofu is a Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) sandbox project idx_f2a64639 that was
created from a fork of Terraform after idx_eabdff12 a licensing change was announced. OpenTofu idx_ce23342b seeks to
maintain backward compatibility with previous versions as it progresses, and is intended to be
a drop-in replacement for Terraform. There may be some use cases where they do not have
one-to-one capabilities, and as both projects evolve individually, that case count is likely to
increase. However, OpenTofu is still a fully functional and production-ready tool for
infrastructure as code.
Ansible
Ansible is capable of virtual machine or Kubernetes deployments, but its strength lies in the
robust configuration capabilities it idx_d663edf4 also has. Ansible will run its tasks against what it calls
hosts, or the infrastructure idx_6d12718b within its inventory. The inventory is user-generated by either
directly passing it into the run command or supplying an inventory file. Ansible organizes its
work into files known as playbooks. Playbooks idx_e304e182 are written in YAML but support Jinja2
templates. Playbooks idx_ef086720 leverage templates via template files. The templating capabilities allow
for the usage of loops and conditions in addition to variables and facts. This gives more
configuration flexibility and allows for efficient procedural operations—for example, only
installing a package on the host if it's not already present, or getting the IP of the host and then
plugging it into the rendered template during execution.

Now that we know more about templating and " * as code " technologies, let's look at how to
pick and choose a technology.
Choosing and using your templating technology
The best advice we authors can give you for determining which observability and templating
technology to adopt is this: do the idx_df2caacf needful; use what you need, not what you think you need. In
other words, solve the problems you have, not the problems you think you will have or don't
have yet. That doesn't mean completely abandon the idea of flexibility, but it does mean
prioritizing what you know you need when deciding what to integrate. To identify what the
needful is, first identify who your users are. Remember, the purpose of a platform is to provide
the correct set of capabilities to the end users, that is, the software developers building the
customer-facing or internal apps. A platform needs to be purpose-built, or else it is just more
infrastructure. For more on building a platform as a product, see Platform Engineering for
Architects, another Packt title by Max Koerbächer, Andreas Grabner, and Hilliary Lipsig.
Once you have your users identified, you can then conduct user interviews and create critical
user journeys. This will allow you to identify where your users can benefit from templates and
other platform capabilities, and what the needed capabilities will look like.
From there, use a crawl, walk, run approach. Start with the most straightforward use case and
the technology to match. Once that is in use, work on the more advanced cases. For example,
you may start with Prometheus templates and then later move on to having Helm manage
those templates, and finally, use Argo CD to manage the deployments and changes to them. Or
you could combine Helm and Kustomize to get the ideal user experience for the platform users.
Some quick decisions you can make based on our recommendations are as follows:
If you need multi-architecture-capable observability, choose Prometheus and Grafana
If you want to manage deployments with complex inheritance requirements in
Kubernetes, choose Helm
If you need multi-cloud infrastructure management, choose Terraform or OpenTofu
Most of these tools are not mutually exclusive, and with the open source options, you are not
vendor-locked. However, even across idx_2cfb98e3 observability SaaS vendors, you may find a mix-and-
match approach or the ability to migrate from one to another if it becomes necessary. Mixing,
matching, expanding, and migrating will all come down to how you decide to manage the
lifecycle of the templates your platform supports.

How to life cycle templates
If there is one truth in software engineering, it is that when you think you have finished, you

chunks.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
chunks.heading: Chapter 5 174
chunks.content:
have not. There's always a dependency that needs to be bumped for security patches, a bug
that needs to be fixed, or some other change coming down the pipeline. While some things
may change very slowly, or idx_4c0cc350 very rarely, it's still important to have a clear versioning strategy
and change management in place—in other words, a life cycle.
Templates are functionally the same as code; thus, the lifecycling of templates is a solved
problem. Treat them the same as idx_765fa847 your code. Like other code, they have a repository, and they
have to be cared for: stored, documented, versioned, and tracked.
In this context, your templates are no different from any other utility code. There isn't a hall of
AWS Lambda scripts; in fact, it isn't generally valuable to try to reuse such specialized code.
Perhaps it can be shared within a team or community, but the environment it lives in is ever-
changing. After version changes impact its utility, it must be adapted or decommissioned.
For boilerplate, it's even more straightforward. Release a new version of the SDK and let the
magic of libraries in software do the work for you and the engineers who consume your SDK.
Here you will find a comprehensive, but likely incomplete, list of all the ways you can approach
template life cycle management.
Change tracking
The key thing to know about templates is that when we in the industry talk about * as code,
templating is a cornerstone of that idx_10ce255f concept. Templates are typically stored in version control
such as Git and managed as source code.
For day-to-day management, the principles of GitOps apply. If a template is updated, your
desired state may not match the actual state; a GitOps tool such as Argo CD can help to ensure
that the changes you've made are populated to the correct locations—for example, pushing the
updates directly or making them available for pull models to catch the changes and bring them
in. Push is more event-driven, but pull is more secure, so both have their place in the
management of * as code.
There are automation-based solutions for catching changes between the base templates and
the rendered templates or repositories where the templates are invoked.
One such tool is the Renovate Bot. Renovate idx_863f4644 can be used to instrument GitHub repositories to
catch dependency updates and automatically make PRs to projects to bump the dependency
version. The repository that needs to inherit the changes is the one Renovate is configured
against, and the repository where idx_3a17863b the changes will come from will be listed in the data sources
configuration. For more information on the specifics of how Renovate works, we refer you to

chunks.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
chunks.heading: Chapter 5 176
chunks.content:
Chapter 5 176
the official documentation (https://docs.renovatebot.com/key-concepts/how-renovate-
works/).
This approach works for template changes, SDK updates, or boilerplate changes. The Renovate
automation tools catch differences between template versions (and they should be versioned)
and the version the rendered templates are using. When it catches drift, it will make PRs to
keep the two in sync. There are several ways to leverage Renovate, but the GitHub action is
where we recommend getting started (https://github.com/renovatebot/github-action).
If you've never used it before, Renovate can use a variety of data sources, and commonly will be
set to use GitHub releases as one of those sources. If you're publishing an SDK, when a new
version is released, if the release is created in GitHub, the Renovate Bot will catch the new
release for the repositories where it is a dependency, and similarly make a PR to bump to the
newer release version in that repo.
Renovate is also a great tool to use to manage Helm subcharts; the latest information on Helm
3 compatibility and eventual Helm 4 compatibility can be found in the official documentation
(https://docs.renovatebot.com/modules/manager/helmv3/).
To catch template differences for rendered templates in use, besides GitOps tools, a policy
engine such as Kyverno can also be idx_2d3da4bf used. This will help to catch whether changes are
attempted through an unexpected method, such as direct edits from a user. While the
existence of a platform and its capabilities should reduce instances of human intervention or
human-initiated edits, these things still do happen, and a policy engine can help to prevent
them entirely, or simply notify of the event, depending on the configuration.
Usage tracking
Another key part of lifecycling is knowing idx_31683b9e when it's time to deprecate a resource. Maintaining a
template or pieces of boilerplate costs time and money, so you need to be sure that it's worth
the investment; or, if you're removing a template for technical or business reasons, be sure that
it's safe to do so.
If you're removing boilerplate code, that can be more straightforward as it was directly cloned
into the end environment and can continue to exist without any need for upstream
management and maintenance. It becomes the responsibility of the implementing team.
However, for templates, especially for Helm charts, this requires more careful consideration.
That consideration should include whether or not the chart is in use. But how can you measure
usage and determine whether templates are in use?
If you're using Helm, Komodor has idx_d4323a0b created a plugin called Helm Dashboard, which can be
installed on your Kubernetes cluster and idx_a2fac1dc will show you which charts are currently in use:
https://github.com/komodorio/helm-dashboard.

177 Democratizing Observability: A Primer to Self-Service Platforms
Finally, if you are using the Backstage idx_bce43075 developer portal as your IDP, and your templates are
registered to the software catalog, it has functionality that can measure the usage of those
templates, allowing you to make data-driven decisions. If you're finding that a template is
never or rarely used, it's a good candidate for deprecation.
What is the role of the platform?
It's up to the platform team to consult with stakeholders and ultimately define the standards
of observability tools and data collection. While individual development teams can also
leverage templates, the platform acts as a unification layer to ensure consistency and ease. By
providing the templates and standards along with enforcement, the platform ensures best
practices are followed. Templates idx_63f7c4a0 and boilerplate don't just assist in democratizing best
practices; they can also encourage and promote observability-driven development. This does
not shift left the accountability, but rather expands it left, providing the framework for
developers to incorporate observability as early as possible in the development cycle.
That enforcement and consistency treat all aspects of applications and tooling equally. From
the platform perspective, everything is an app (including parts of the platform itself). That is to
say, whatever best practices you apply to your customer-facing apps, you must also apply to
your AI and other applications.
Enforcement of the maturity models
In the Platform Engineering for Architects book, Hilliary defined maturity models as the
sociotechnical side of an IDP. These are going to be very subjective but essentially become the
minimum set of standards an idx_59f7977c application must meet to be onboarded to the IDP. Through the
use of policy engines and static analysis tools, a platform can shape the landscape of the
software being developed within an organization.
A simple maturity model for onboarding a new application to the IDP may look like a checklist
of tasks to be completed:
Kubernetes object definitions are labeled or annotated.
Prometheus alerts are configured.
SLOs are defined.
Alerts are routed to the appropriate service.
A Grafana dashboard configuration has been submitted.
Troubleshooting guides have been written and approved.
You may have other tasks to idx_ca0eb814 add to this list, but it's a starting point to help you develop the
standards your IDP defines, uses, and enforces.

The platform is the unifying layer
With the platform providing the golden path, it must also become the central hub for all truth.
This includes application definitions, access idx_9b3dfdc6 controls, and the observability data. The platform
needs to provide distinct value that brings users back and makes them happy to use it.
Centralized observability is just one example of the capabilities an IDP will need to have;
another is access controls.
Access controls are one of the most critical pieces of the platform capability. Democratization
of data cannot come at the expense of security and compliance requirements. The platform
must define and enforce least privilege for the observability data it stores and makes available
to users.
Most observability tooling idx_c6fdd1ea you would integrate into your platform supports access controls,
often called Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) or Identity Access Management (IAM). For
the idx_5552cd2b context of building an IDP with robust observability capabilities, you won't want to
manage access controls in multiple places. You will need to choose technologies that integrate
with the solutions already in place.
Grafana is an excellent example of this, as while you can manage RBAC directly, it supports
application plugins to leverage existing access control systems such as OAuth configured via
GitHub, GitLab, Okta, Google, and more. It has additional flexibility in that it can connect to
multiple data sources, such as databases, individual machines, or blob storage, allowing it to
act as a single point of entry for all data within an IDP. It's also architecture-agnostic, so if you
have a mix of architecture types, you won't need to have multiple data visualization tools. The
flexibility of Grafana makes it a good choice if you don't want your platform to be opinionated
on where observability data is shipped or how it's structured when stored, allowing teams to
self-service the Grafana configurations and plugins they need. Managing the Grafana
instance's availability would provide the flexibility your development teams need without
losing out on core platform functionality.
Grafana also supports the use of pre-made dashboards from templates, as well as allowing
user-defined dashboards. Here, we quickly used a template to visualize observability data

Using or building the right tools to make the right data available, but only to the right people
or systems, will be core to your observability strategy. Any AIOps implementation will need to
be gated with appropriate access, which we'll cover further in later chapters as well. Now that
we've established how the idx_4e5c378e platform standardizes observability data collection, let's look at
how AI can augment the platform's enforcement capabilities and why the platform must treat
AI workloads with the same observability rigor as any other application.
Use cases for the integration of AI into the IDP
Where can an AIOps implementation help accelerate platform growth and offload tasks from
the platform team? While we idx_bf85010f can't possibly be exhaustive in our recommendations, we do
have a few places where we think AIOps can help, and it's not just acting as a user-facing
chatbot either.
The first is as part of the code quality enforcement arm. While traditional linters or even
custom GitHub actions can go a long way to ensure boilerplate code examples and platform
requirements for handling observability are met, they are still limited in their flexibility.
There are even products such as SonarQube that help idx_a0d736d8 platform engineering teams to ensure
quality gates are satisfied. But the same challenges we find with maintaining any automation
become readily apparent. Your automation is only as good as its programming and will be
limited in what it can do to what you've had time to write.
Here is where AI can find its time in the limelight. As we discussed in Chapter 2, an LLM-based
AI tool has far fewer limitations and can make inferences while also adhering to a set of
supplied instructions.
181 Democratizing Observability: A Primer to Self-Service Platforms
For example, AI can act as a multi-architecture bridge. It's almost impossible to apply the exact
same standards to observability for a virtual machine-based environment as for a Kubernetes
environment, so AI can act as the bridge between them to help normalize the data, or act as a
tool to sample or sanitize where other standard tools might not be so easily adaptable.
Data timeliness and quality are important, but no tool is entirely perfect. Prometheus can, in
some configurations, crash and lose data. Accepted idx_79242995 sources such as CloudWatch are known to
have strict rules for log timing, which idx_1b1b473d can create ingestion problems or omissions if time zones
are not properly accounted for in configurations. Serverless, low-code, and no-code metrics are
often shallow in scope and poorly communicated. And sometimes data may be lost due to

chunks.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
chunks.heading: Chapter 5 180
chunks.content:
events outside anyone's control, such as a natural disaster.
In these cases, AI may be very well positioned to handle unreliable or incomplete data but will
need to be given data and sources along with explicit constraints or instructions.
Instruction files and giving your AI direction
Instructions are provided via instruction idx_c21ebed5 files, and there are many ways to make instruction
files available to an AI system. For example, there's a project within the Linux Foundation
known as agents.md, which is a standardization effort around Markdown files added to code
bases with instructions that are useful to anyone, but specifically intended to help AI agents be
successful when interacting with a code base. There are no universally expected fields for an
instruction file, but there are best practices for writing a good one.
First, structure your file. Break it into topics and leverage Markdown formatting to break the
instructions into segments. For example, build instructions and test instructions should be
different headings.
Second, be as detailed and specific as possible. Just like when writing a README for a human,
the more details you provide, the less guesswork the AI needs to do. If you want your agent to
assume a certain role, task, or objective, be sure to include that information; that specificity can
help the AI to come back with better responses. If you want a specific output, such as what we
indicated with our data normalization use case, then that output format should also be in the
instruction file. Anything that is important for the AI to know, including your expectations,
belongs in your instruction file.
Third, let the AI know what it can and cannot do. If it can reach out to the internet, include
that. If it cannot reach out to the internet, include that in the instructions as well. Your
instruction files are the first line of governance for the AI system, and you can make it aware of
security and compliance requirements, as well as what data sources it has access to, in these
files.

Chapter 5 182
Finally, when you are building out your instructions, you will want to test them and adjust
them. It's also important to keep them current with new information that your AI agent needs
to know.
For example, instructions for an idx_f6baff12 observability agent may look something like this rudimentary
example:
# AGENTS.md file
## Agent Persona
- You are a Site Reliability Engineer in a Kubernetes environment.
## Agent Constraints
- We are a SOC 2 Compliant Company
- You do not have external internet connectivity
## Desired Response Format
- Place investigation details into Jira
- Remove any data that could be PII
- When a solution is identified, open a pull request in GitHub following any
relevant contributor guidelines.
## Data Sources
- There is a Prometheus instance on the cluster
- There are logs being collected with Fluentbit
- OpenTelemetry is also in use
## Important Cluster Information
- All software has been installed with Helm charts
- All observability data should have labels and other metadata.
With proper instructions, AI agents can be more efficient and get to work faster. And by setting
expectations about the system it is working on, the AI can start detecting trends and patterns
in the data. From there, if you are in a situation where you have missing observability data, an
AI system can infer whether there's reason to suspect that there's a problem that extends
beyond the monitoring stack itself.
However, it's important to set your own expectations. If the data doesn't have strong
cardinality, such as labels and metadata, and the AI agent or assistant has never seen the
system before, the quality of the inference will be diminished; but once both of those are true
and the AI system is tuned, its judgment to identify and investigate large-scale issues can
generally be trusted. We will go over fine-tuning and its benefits in depth in Chapter 9.
A well-tuned AI system will bring insights to the users, which may often augment or extend
their existing expertise. For example, an AI can help with the following:
Best-practice recognition •

Misconfiguration detection
Data capture at preproduction through to runtime
Cost management
However, even with proper tuning, we can't let our AI run completely unattended. This is
where the platform must treat AI equally and apply the same security and access control
standards as it would to any application. The AI system must be observable and subjected to
governance; this is how we can idx_3f8c4d74 prove that the system is performing safely and meeting
expectations. Now that we've examined what observability looks like within the platform, let's
apply that to an AIOps implementation.
A reliable AI is an observable AI
A good IDP is customer zero to itself. The golden paths must be equally achievable for the

product that provides them. AIOps is part of that customer zero model. It will be developed,
deployed, and monitored to the same idx_124f388e standards as anything else, with the goal of becoming
another capability of the platform for engineering teams to leverage. The capability to use and
benefit from an AI agent must be part of that centralized experience.
For an AIOps implementation to be useful, it must be accurate. Measuring the success and
accuracy of AI is a new challenge, but the concepts we have already discussed for observability
still apply. There are new standards when it comes to metrics for AI performance that are good
to keep in mind, and also new tooling, but at the end of the day, these purpose-built tools
recycle best practices.
In a Kubernetes environment, AI workloads are just Pods at the end of the day. So the usual
standards for Kubernetes workloads apply. You'll want to watch Pod health, such as CPU and
memory usage, as well as checking for crashes, restarts, or other general health problems.
Similar to most other applications, your AI applications will have performance metrics.
Request and response latency are key among them, but so are measurements of accuracy.
For AI workloads, these idx_a3df42e0 metrics will be critical to understanding whether your AI is providing
the right value to your organization:
Inference speed
Time to first token (TTFT)

Operations per minute (OPM)
Response accuracy

Knowing the metrics we need is great, but how do we determine what the measurements for
those metrics should be, and once we have those measurements, how do we make sure the AI
is performing as expected?
A good open source tool for benchmarking your AI system is GuideLLM (https://
github.com/vllm-project/guidellm), part of the vLLM project. GuideLLM is a platform for
evaluating how language models perform under real workloads and configurations. It can
operate on real or synthetically generated multimodal datasets and gives you clear insights
into performance, efficiency, and reliability before deploying LLMs into a production
environment. GuideLLM is a good starting point for benchmarking and optimizing your LLMs
as it also puts a focus on idx_3002317f the key metrics discussed previously: TTFT, inter-token latency
(ITL), output distributions, and dataset-driven variations. While there idx_2d7e912b are some industry
standards around what good metrics for performance look like that are emerging, there's not a
one-size-fits-all metric. Different models perform differently for the same task, and the same
model can perform differently across tasks of different complexity. This is because various
prompts can rightly need longer response times, more tokens, and more exchanges with an end
user. Time and tokens will be two aspects of performance and reliability to monitor as your
model processes prompts, and establishing a baseline and catching deviations from the
baseline will be critical to proper model observability. It's best to benchmark your model with
tests that mimic production, and evaluate the metrics of real use against those benchmarks.
You'll know what good looks like for your system over time with regular human review, and
ultimately, you'll be able to set up alerts and tune them. A good practice would be a weekly ops
review meeting to help define targets and alerts, instead of alerting right away and possibly
creating a signal that is no more than noise.
Whether you are using GuideLLM or other tools and frameworks, measuring that you're
maintaining the benchmarked performance is harder and requires putting some thought into
the system design for the AI system. Technically speaking, the LLM that powers your AI will be
accessed via an API. Functionally, once an API is in use for your AI agent, it stops being unique
and starts being the same as every other workload in your environment. TTFT becomes simple
math, subtracting the timestamp of the request sent to the API from the time the first token is
sent back. This can be measured with Prometheus rules or OTel.

chunks.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
chunks.heading: Chapter 5 184
chunks.content:
You can build a bespoke API and an AI serving engine, and the OpenAI developer docs have
great references to help do just that. However, there are open source options to save you the

trouble. If you're using vLLM to serve your AI agent, it comes with many metrics already
defined in the framework, ready for use: https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/usage/metrics/
#general-metrics. Also, you can always build out and define your own as needed.
Where most metrics are easily defined as numbers, accuracy may not immediately strike you as
a quantifiable metric. Up next, we'll show you how to measure accuracy and keep measuring it.
Strategies for measuring response accuracy
The challenge with measuring response accuracy is that responses need to be evaluated
regularly; it's not a one-and-done situation. As training data or other data the AI system has
access to increases, there's a reasonable expectation of drift between how the system
responded after initial training idx_5423debb and how it responds later on; however, that drift should be only
due to facts changing, not due to errors. We've identified the following practical strategies for
measuring response accuracy.
Natural language processing scoring
For natural language processing, there are many scoring systems for accuracy: BLEU, ROUGE,
BERT, METEOR, and Perplexity, just to idx_57611c93 name a few, and others may yet emerge. The most well
known are the BLEU and ROUGE systems. The BLEU scoring system is often used for use cases
where the output must be highly precise. If you've noticed that an AI chatbot uses a lot of
words to convey an idea but leaves little room for interpretation, it's likely scoring well against
the BLEU system.
ROUGE prioritizes recall and is intended as the scoring system for cases where summarization
and recall are more critical than output generation. It's a good scoring system for agents that
are parsing and distilling large amounts of observability data.
Of the other scoring systems we've mentioned, the most relevant for AIOps is BERT. It has a
similar scoring methodology to ROUGE but is computationally more expensive and may
provide a more accurate score. We'll spare you the math, but there's a link to a deep-dive article
on how scores for all three of these systems are calculated in the Further reading section of this
chapter.
For the purposes of observability and AIOps, we recommend using the ROUGE or BERT scoring
system to evaluate model performance, should you so choose. Both scoring models use a range
of 0-1. For production systems a score of around 0.8 on the BERT scale and around 0.4 on the
ROUGE scale would be considered on target.
Let's score the DeepSeek R1 model we've been using since Chapter 2 using Python scripts.

Chapter 5 186

determination is made will depend largely on how the response is delivered. For example, if
the response is a Slack message to the team channel raising awareness of a system outage, and

accuracy will likely require some manual process, and potentially some mixture of clever
automation, such as labeling the PRs that were not accurate and running automation to count
them regularly.

solutions to measure the accuracy of the output.
Finally, a third option is to have another AI agent determine whether the response is accurate.
Multi-agent AI orchestration adds some additional technical and financial implications. In
terms of level of effort, the tooling is evolving and it has become easier to support a model
where a separate AI agent acts as a validator, grader, or evaluator of the output of another
agent. You can see this as a teacher who validates and grades the work of a student. The
teacher gives feedback on what seems accurate and what doesn't. Just like humans evaluate
the work of others, the same concept can be applied to AI agents, with the result that those
agents should constantly get better.

PII, which stands for personally identifiable information, is a protected class of information
that may be collected idx_5e3e59b7 during normal operations for a software system. Earlier, we indicated
that you'd likely place your AI agent behind an API. The method for doing this would be
through the implementation of a microservice known as the API gateway. This middleware

The centralized platform becomes the centralized data hub, but the expectation remains that it
still works in service idx_b8a634cf of individual teams and their needs. The platform should provide data in a

How many times have you needed the observability data from 2:36 A.M. on a Tuesday six
months ago? Likely never, but you may have needed the data trends over the same six-month
period. You don't need to keep every single instance of every single metric. Using AI to do basic
data sampling can help to reduce the stored metrics down to means, medians, and modes over
time, and that time can be at whatever level of granularity makes sense for your organization.
By keeping only the data we need, and keeping the valuable information we got from the data
we no longer need, we can shrink our data stores without fearing that we'll miss out on a
critical piece of information. While we wouldn't recommend letting the AI delete data that no
longer needs to be stored, ensuring that it's available to end users who need sampling either
regularly or on demand, with the ability to write the output to a permanent locations, would
allow the platform team to use time to live or other data lifecycling features to automatically
prune old and less valuable data from the databases.
Additionally, if we believe we idx_5f640d2f may have PII in our stored logs or metrics, having an AI agent
crawl through it, sample the logs, and pull out only what's safe and statistically significant
would be faster than having a human try to script the same thing. Letting the AI access, parse,
and surface observability data to make it actionable for a development team is essentially the
perfect task for its capabilities. This brings specific value for an IDP that needs to have a unified
presentation layer that loads quickly, so end users actually want to interact with it.

Essentially, where users of the platform spend idx_0827d0fd most of their day is where data should be sent.

The following are examples of what and where your observability tooling, including AI, may be
pushing data, and who might be consuming that data:
For developers: Push newly detected critical logs directly to developers via their IDE,
dev portal (Backstage), on the PR, or as a daily Slack message, instead of asking them to
learn yet another tool to find data that is relevant to them
For product owners: Push feature adoption metrics to the Jira ticket where the feature
was specified, instead of asking the business to get the data themselves from various
observability tools or dashboards
For performance engineers: Commit the top findings of a recent load test based on
observability data captured during the test to the codebase backing the CI pipeline that
triggered the test
Within your specific industry, there may be other best practices, and if you're using an
observability vendor, they may have some additional recommended best practices as well.
Understanding your security and compliance requirements is critical for knowing where you
should and should not push observability data. Observability is the art of turning data into
information. That information is idx_7c3daaa4 often need-to-know, so you will want to ensure you are
getting the right information, to the right people, in the right way. For example, it is important
to know that a user encountered a 500 error when interacting with the system, but identifying
who the user is is unimportant to getting the issue fixed and should never be included in any
data that is collected and stored.
It's important for any AI systems you're using to also understand and adhere to this principle,
which is why it's critical to put that information in instruction files. We'll talk more about
implementing guardrails and how to secure your AI systems in Chapter 9.
Remember that AI depends on instructions and input and is therefore susceptible to the
principle of garbage in, garbage out (GIGO). By idx_04df4fd8 ensuring your data is well structured and
explained, you avoid a long list of unhappy consequences. Any time an AI-enhanced tool leaks
user data, consider the following:
Was access to user idx_f52567d7 data necessary for it to do its job?
Could that data have been obfuscated?
Could that data have been better structured and explained?
Reasonable implementations should start from an understanding of the information
presented, the risks involved, and the nature of its destination. Where possible, start with the
least possible amount of access and data and increase as it becomes necessary. Don't let the
fear of missing out result in a security incident in your organization.

The four phases of agentic AI
There are many idx_9dcd6f7e definitions given in this book, but let me give you one more from a public
knowledge base entry [1]:
Agentic AI builds on generative AI by enabling software agents to act with
autonomy. IDC defines it as systems that can make decisions, adapt to new
environments, and complete complex tasks with minimal human input. These
systems reason, learn from experience, and interact with their environment—often
coordinating across multiple agents—to continuously optimize outcomes.
NVIDIA, known for manufacturing the specialized computer chips that power many of the
data centers that run AI workloads, describes the four phases [2] that agentic AI goes through:
Perceive: Gather and interpret data from the environment or system.
Reason: Use LLMs and possibly retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to plan

Act: Integrate with external tools and software to execute actions.
Learn: Use feedback loops to improve future decisions through reinforcement learning.

connect with your observability platform in each individual phase.

logs, metrics, or traces. Modern observability can be used in multiple tasks in the explained

Bug tracking
A lot of information idx_957d2728 can be found in your issues and bug tracking systems. Whether this is in
Jira, GitLab, or GitHub Issues, it's a data source that can tell us whether somebody in the past
worked on a similar problem. An MCP server connected to that system can execute queries to
find bug tickets based on a similar problem description in the impacted application or services.
It can then analyze whether and how the problem was fixed in the past and provide this
information back to the developer. This idx_bf579516 saves a lot of time in identifying the next step, as it
could be that the problem was solved in the past, and we already know how to do it.
Status pages
You may idx_93ddbd4e remember October 20, 2025, as the day half the internet stood still. Why? Because
there was a major impact across the AWS US East Region. Whether it is AWS, Azure, GCP,
Salesforce, or any other third-party SaaS offering, the first thing to do is to check the status
pages of those services you are dependent on. If there is a known ongoing issue, then this could
be the root cause of your problem and will trigger a different course of action, as if all those
third-party services are running healthy. Integrating the information about status pages into
your AI agent allows for validating this additional data source. One option would be to use an
MCP server that connects to Downdetector [3], which is a service that provides real-time
problem and outage monitoring for a wide range of publicly accessible APIs.
CRM
Whether a problem idx_a75fcc59 impacts 1,000 users or just one should have no impact on how you
prioritize the problem. But on the other hand, when you have lots of fires to put out, it's
important to focus on the problem with the biggest impact. The biggest impact can mean that
a single premium user who is impacted by a new feature needs more attention than 100 non-
paying users who experience a performance degradation.
While idx_85e2e9e5 your real user monitoring (RUM) from your observability platform can tell you which
users, identified by user ID, are impacted, the CRM system can tell you how important those
users are for your business.
